moves.spoken: Black meets the king's pawn with the Scandinavian, challenging our center at once.
We develop the knight to c3 with tempo, hitting the queen on d5 and gaining a free move.
teaches: develop with tempo against the early queen

moves.spoken: The queen tucks to d6 — a modern, fully respectable branch of the Scandinavian — and we seize the full center with d4.
teaches: Qd6 is a legitimate modern line

moves.spoken: Nothing exotic is needed: we simply develop and control the center, and let Black prove his setup.
Black leans on the d4-pawn and eyes the pin with the bishop to g4 — the classic pressure we have to answer.
So we play the mildly ugly but effective h3, taking the g4-square away from the bishop before the pin can happen.
Threat handled, we develop actively — the bishop to c4, raking toward f7 and supporting a future d5 break.
The bishop to g5 is the active square; parking it on e3 would be a touch too passive here.
More quiet prophylaxis: a4 denies Black the b5 push with tempo and the queenside fianchetto that follows — the kind of preventive move you see constantly at master level.
teaches: a4 stops b5 before it starts

moves.spoken: The idea behind the retreat: reroute the knight to e2, then to g3, which frees us to play c3 and secure d4 permanently. A backward-looking move can be exactly right.
plans: Ne2-g3 then c3 to cement d4

moves.spoken: The queen to b4 looks intimidating, but the grab on b2 is simply unthinkable — so there's nothing real behind it.
teaches: a scary-looking sortie with no bite

moves.spoken: b3 solves everything at once: no worry about the capture on b2, and if the knight harasses from a5 our bishop just drops to d3 and aims at the king.
The queen on b4 is stranded in no man's land now; we can trade on e7 or tuck the bishop back to d2, both comfortable.
The rook to e1 x-rays the black queen down the file, quietly discouraging the e5 freeing break.
teaches: x-ray pressure to prevent a break

moves.spoken: The knight to g3 completes that x-ray idea, both pieces trained on the e-file.
The knight jumps into e4, a superb central post, and White is now clearly the more comfortable side.
The knight swings to c5 and we begin piling onto the queenside.
b6 shoves the knight but leaves lasting holes on the queenside — weaknesses we intend to make him pay for later.
Rather than grab anything, we reroute the knight back to d3, heading for e5. It looks mysterious, but it's pure piece-optimization — hunting the best central square for every piece.
teaches: maneuver to your best squares before striking

moves.spoken: The knight settles on e5, the commanding outpost, while keeping the other knight free so the queen can reach the kingside for an attack.
The bishop drops to d3, trained once again on Black's king.
f6 only makes Black more passive and, above all, weakens the e6-pawn — the new target.
We bring the knight back to g4 with tempo: the e6-pawn is falling and the black queen is running out of squares.
teaches: retreat with tempo to win the weakness

moves.spoken: The rook swings to e4 to collect the pawn — once e6 goes, the whole position caves.
The trap springs: the black queen has no squares. A pawn to g3 will hem it in, the rook on e6 covers d6, and the knight guards the rest — so the queen has to be given up for two pieces.
teaches: net the queen by taking its last squares

moves.spoken: That's why the rook went to e6 — not just to take the pawn but to deny the queen its escape to d6. With both knights loose, we move one with a threat to win material, pin the defender with the bishop to c4, and route the knight via g5 to e6 to crash through on g7.
teaches: deny the escape square, then collect

moves.spoken: A clean finish and a resignation — the plan carried from opening to endgame without a single mysterious move.

To recap: against the popular Qd6 Scandinavian we stop the pin with h3, halt b5 with a4, then reroute the knight to e2 and g3 so c3 can permanently secure d4 — retreats and all. After the trade on e7 the rook to e1 x-rays the queen, the knights improve through g3, e4, c5 and back to d3, and every move simply optimizes a piece.
